# Results — Study 713 ("Classic cars are an asset class that beats equities")

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Do collector cars beat the
S&P? We test the strongest tradable version of the claim: a collector-car **price index**
(hardcoded, cited, **approximate** — a labelled proxy, not a live feed, reconstructed from
HAGI Top / Knight Frank Luxury Investment Index / Hagerty reporting) and the only **listed**
ways to buy the trade (Ferrari `RACE`, Aston Martin `AML.L`), benchmarked against the S&P on
**both** a total-return (`SPY`) and a price-only (`^GSPC`) clock. Offline & deterministic;
run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Car index | **Hardcoded, cited, approximate** annual price level (base 100 @ 2005-12-31), reconstructed from public HAGI Top / Knight Frank LII / Hagerty reporting — see [`docs/references.md`](references.md). **A PROXY, not a feed.** |
| Equity proxies | `RACE` (Ferrari, NYSE, from its 2015-10 IPO) · `AML.L` (Aston Martin Lagonda, LSE, from its 2018-10 IPO) — month-end Adj Close (total return) via yfinance, cached under `_cache/` |
| Benchmarks | `SPY` (dividend-adjusted → **total return**) and `^GSPC` (**price-only** S&P 500), month-end via yfinance |
| As-of | 2025-12-31 (month-end; no partial-year bar) |
| Index window | 2005-12 → 2025-12 (20 annual returns) · equity proxies from their respective IPOs |

> **Why a proxy, stated as a decision.** Real collector-car indices (the HAGI Top Index,
> the classic-car sleeve of the Knight Frank Luxury Investment Index, the Hagerty Price
> Guide / Market Rating) are **not freely API-available**. Rather than fabricate a live
> tape we (a) hardcode a small, clearly-cited, **approximate** annual series whose *shape* —
> a 2009–2015 melt-up, a 2016–2020 plateau, a 2022 bump and a 2023–24 cooling — is the
> load-bearing public fact, and (b) test the **tradable** equity proxies a public investor
> can actually buy. A carmaker's equity is **not** the auction price of a 250 GTO; the
> tickers are labelled proxies throughout.

## Half 1 — did the cars beat the S&P? (car index vs S&P, priced fairly)

The (approximate, cited) collector-car index, year-end levels base 100:

| year | 2005 | 2008 | 2011 | 2013 | 2015 | 2018 | 2020 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| level | 100 | 140 | 205 | 300 | **372** | 378 | 380 | 480 | **490** | 470 | 476 |

A powerful **2009–2015 melt-up** (roughly ×3.7), then a decade of **plateau**. Headline
risk/return, priced **both ways** (the car index is a *price* index, so `^GSPC` price-only is
the apples-to-apples race; `SPY` total-return is the equity you'd actually own):

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Collector-car index** | **+8.11%** | 8.8% | 0.96 | −4.1% |
| S&P 500 — **total return** (`SPY`) | **+10.91%** | 17.3% | 0.72 | −36.8% |
| S&P 500 — **price only** (`^GSPC`) | **+8.88%** | 17.1% | 0.61 | −38.5% |

**The cars lost the race** — even against the *price-only* S&P (8.11% vs 8.88%), and by
~3 points/yr against the S&P you'd actually hold (10.91%). The mean annual excess is:

| benchmark | mean annual excess (index − S&P) | *t* | p | n |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| vs total return (`SPY`) | **−3.97%/yr** | **−0.90** | 0.380 | 20 |
| vs price only (`^GSPC`) | −1.94%/yr | −0.44 | 0.663 | 20 |

No *t* ≥ 2 in the cars' favour on either clock — the honest read is "no evidence cars beat
stocks, and the point estimate is negative."

## The smoothness trap — the "low risk" is an appraisal artifact

The car index's Sharpe (0.96) *beats* the S&P's (0.72) — but only because its volatility is
measured off a smoothed, serially-correlated appraisal series. Geltner first-order AR(1)
un-smoothing $r^u_t = (r_t - \rho r_{t-1})/(1-\rho)$:

| | value |
|---|--:|
| AR(1) ρ of annual car returns | **+0.638** (a smooth, laggy index) |
| annual vol — **reported** | 8.8% |
| annual vol — **de-smoothed** | **18.6%** (now *above* the S&P's 17.3%) |
| Sharpe — **reported** | 0.96 |
| Sharpe — **de-smoothed** | **0.34** (now *below* the S&P's 0.72) |

Un-smoothed, the car index is **more** volatile than the S&P with roughly **half** the
risk-adjusted return. The calm ride was the reporting, not the asset — the same bias that
flatters real-estate and private-equity indices.

## Half 2 — the tradable proxies vs the S&P (the only thing you can buy)

Monthly Adj Close, Newey-West (6-lag) alpha vs `SPY` total return. **Labelled proxies.**

| series | CAGR | ann. vol | Sharpe | max DD | alpha/yr | beta | NW *t*(α) | p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **RACE** (Ferrari) | +22.58% | 28.3% | 0.86 | −29.1% | +10.24% | 1.00 | **+1.28** | 0.202 |
| **AML.L** (Aston Martin) | **−43.13%** | 55.2% | −0.70 | **−98.3%** | −47.87% | 1.54 | **−2.78** | 0.007 |
| SPY (total return) | +10.61% | 14.8% | 0.76 | −50.8% | — | — | — | — |

A **barbell, not a signal.** Ferrari posted a large alpha that does **not** clear
significance (*t* = +1.28) — and it is a high-margin luxury-goods brand, not a resale-price
feed. Aston Martin posted a *significantly negative* alpha (*t* = −2.78) and a −98% drawdown.
Two "collector-car" equities, opposite signs: **no coherent, tradable alpha** — just
idiosyncratic single-stock risk.

## Half 3 — the carry/illiquidity haircut (what owning the metal costs)

The pitch never charges the friction. An auction round-trip costs ~**22%** (buyer's premium
+ seller's commission, transport/inspection folded in), amortised over a ~**7-year** hold,
plus ~**2.5%/yr** carry (specialist insurance + climate storage + servicing). Charged once on
the index's gross CAGR:

| | value |
|---|--:|
| gross CAGR (index) | +8.11%/yr |
| − auction round-trip drag (22% over 7y) | −3.49%/yr |
| − insurance / storage / servicing carry | −2.50%/yr |
| **= NET CAGR a real owner earns** | **+1.73%/yr** |

The 8.1% gross *that already lost to the S&P* falls to **~1.7%/yr** — savings-account
territory — once you pay to transact and hold the car. And unlike a stock, a car pays **no
dividend** while you wait; it charges you rent.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

A deterministic, fixed-seed "boom-then-plateau" path (planted +16%/yr for a decade, then
+1%/yr, σ = 6%/yr, seed 713): the engine recovers the planted up-sign and a finite Sharpe —
peak ≈ 388 → end ≈ 381, recovered CAGR **+7.05%**, Sharpe 1.05, `sign_ok = 1`. The harness
can bank a planted signal, so a null on the real tape is a real null, not a broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE (it *under*-performs).** Over 2005–2025 the car index returned ~8.1%/yr
  vs ~10.9%/yr for the S&P (total return) and ~8.9%/yr price-only; the annual excess is
  **−4.0%/yr (t = −0.90)** vs TR — no evidence cars beat stocks. The flattering Sharpe (0.96)
  is an appraisal-smoothing artifact: **de-smoothed it is 0.34**, below the S&P's 0.72, with
  *higher* true volatility.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Net of a 22% auction round-trip + 2.5%/yr carry the gross 8.1%
  collapses to **~1.7%/yr** (cash-like); the only buyable proxies are a barbell — a juggernaut
  (RACE, no significant alpha) and a wreck (AML.L, significantly negative, −98% drawdown).
  Illiquid, bespoke, no scalable book.
- **"Cars beat equities?" — BUSTED.** On total return, on *de-smoothed* risk-adjusted return,
  on drawdown *and* net-of-cost, the S&P wins. The price-only near-tie evaporates once you
  count the dividends stocks pay and the carry cars charge. The few who "got rich" bought a
  specific blue-chip chassis before 2015 and sold near the top — survivorship, not an asset class.

> **Caveat (named, not buried).** The car index here is a **small, hardcoded, approximate**
> reconstruction of public reporting — its *level path/shape* is defensible but its precise
> year-end values are not a live feed. The equity proxies are exactly that — proxies for
> "owning the car trade," not the auction price of a car — and each starts at its IPO (a
> stated look-ahead limit). Both limitations push the verdict toward humility, not toward a
> stronger claim: nothing here says cars beat stocks, and several lines say the opposite.
